(a) Requirement.—
        (1) In general.—On the 270th day after the date of the enactment of this Act, and on each succeeding anniversary of such 270th day, each satellite carrier shall submit an annual report to the Federal Communications Commission setting forth—
            (A) each local market in which it—
                (i) retransmits signals of 1 or more television broadcast stations with a community of license in that market; 
                (ii) has commenced providing such signals in the preceding 1-year period; and 
                (iii) has ceased to provide such signals in the preceding 1-year period; and  
            (B) detailed information regarding the use and potential use of satellite capacity for the retransmission of local signals in each local market.  
        (2) Termination.—The requirement under paragraph (1) shall cease after each satellite carrier has submitted 5 reports under such paragraph.  
    (b) FCC Study; Report.—
        (1) Study.—If no satellite carrier files a request for a certification under section 342 of the Communications Act of 1934 (as added by section 206 of this title) within 270 days 
after the date of the enactment of this Act, the Federal Communications Commission shall initiate a study of—
            (A) incentives that would induce a satellite carrier to provide the signals of 1 or more television broadcast stations licensed to provide signals in local markets in which the satellite carrier does not provide such signals; and 
            (B) the economic and satellite capacity conditions affecting delivery of local signals by satellite carriers to these markets.  
        (2) Report.—Within 1 year after the date of the initiation of the study under paragraph (1), the Federal Communications Commission shall submit a report to the appropriate Congressional committees containing its findings, conclusions, and recommendations.  
    (c) Definitions.—In this section—
        (1) the terms “local market” and “satellite carrier” have the meaning given such terms in section 339(d) of the Communications Act of 1934 (47 U.S.C. 339(d)); and 
        (2) the term “television broadcast station” has the meaning given such term in section 325(b)(7) of such Act (47 U.S.C. 325(b)(7)).

fable.w: The tempting reading is that satellite carriers (outside parties) submitting annual reports to the FCC amounts to participation. But these are mandatory compliance and information filings, not consultation or comment before a federal decision. The FCC study does not require outside input, and its report goes to Congressional committees, which are inside the federal government. No rulemaking, hearing, advisory body, or right to sue is created.
fable.s: the Federal Communications Commission shall submit a report to the appropriate Congressional committees containing its findings, conclusions, and recommendations.

qwen_block.w: This section requires satellite carriers to submit reports to the FCC and the FCC to submit a report to Congress. Both satellite carriers (as applicants/reporters) and Congress are not involved in a participatory decision-making process as defined. The carriers are merely reporting data, which is akin to an application or regulatory filing, not consultation. The FCC's report to Congress is an internal government communication, as Congress is inside the federal government. There is no requirement for the FCC to consult with the public, states, or other outside entities before making a decision.
qwen_block.s: the Federal Communications Commission shall submit a report to the appropriate Congressional committees containing its findings, conclusions, and recommendations.

opus.w: The carriers' annual reports are a duty to disclose information, not consultation or coordination with outsiders before a federal decision. The FCC study ends in a report to the appropriate congressional committees, and Congress is inside the federal government. The section has no comment period, public hearing, advisory panel with outside members, or right to sue.
opus.s: each satellite carrier shall submit an annual report to the Federal Communications Commission setting forth—
opus.b: 1. **Tempting but wrong reading:** Satellite carriers are private companies outside the federal government, and they must submit annual reports to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC). That can look like outside parties taking part in agency work. It fails the definition because these reports are a compliance duty to disclose data. The carriers are not consulted before any FCC decision, and there is no comment period, hearing, advisory body or right to sue. The FCC's study and its report to the congressional committees stay entirely inside the federal government.

qwen_chat.w: This section mandates that satellite carriers submit annual reports to the FCC. This is a regulatory reporting requirement, not a participatory process where outside parties consult with the government to influence a decision. The definition excludes applications and implies that mere reporting or compliance does not constitute participation. The subsequent study by the FCC and report to Congress are internal government actions.
qwen_chat.s: (a) Requirement.— (1) In general.—On the 270th day after the date of the enactment of this Act, and on each succeeding anniversary of such 270th day, each satellite carrier shall submit an annual report to the Federal Communications Commission setting forth— (A) each local market in which it— (i) retransmits signals of 1 or more television broadcast stations with a community of license in that market; (ii) has commenced providing such signals in the preceding 1-year period; and (iii) has ceased to provide such signals in the preceding 1-year period; and (B) detailed information regarding the use and potential use of satellite capacity for the retransmission of local signals in each local market.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the requirement for satellite carriers (outside entities) to submit annual reports to the FCC constitutes "participation" because it involves outside parties providing information to the government. However, the definition explicitly excludes "applications for benefits or grants" and generally treats reporting requirements imposed on regulated entities as compliance mechanisms rather than participatory decision-making processes. The carriers are not being consulted to help the FCC make a policy decision; they are being mandated to provide data for regulatory oversight. The FCC's subsequent study and report to Congress are internal government actions (reporting to Congress is explicitly "No"). There is no advisory board, public comment period, consultation with states/tribes, or right to sue granted in this section.
